analysis.one_liner: Lets people sue over COVID relief law violations and suspends forced arbitration during the pandemic.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a hearing, markup, or vote in the House Judiciary Committee and died when the 117th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would give any individual the right to sue in federal court for harm caused by violations of the COVID relief laws — the CARES Act, the Families First Coronavirus Response Act, and the 2021 supplemental relief law [S2] [S3]. It would also make pre-dispute arbitration agreements and class-action waivers unenforceable for employment, consumer, antitrust, and civil rights disputes from the start of the pandemic emergency until 180 days after it ends [S2] [S3]. Arbitration clauses, which are standard in employment and consumer contracts, force workers and customers into private one-on-one proceedings instead of court or class action [S3].
analysis.who_benefits: Workers, consumers, and civil rights claimants gain the ability to enforce federal COVID relief laws in court and, during the covered emergency period, to take employment, consumer, antitrust, and civil rights disputes to court or join class actions instead of being funneled into individual arbitration [S2] [S3].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Workers, consumers, and civil rights plaintiffs

how_it_helps.text: Creates an explicit right for any individual harmed by a violation of the CARES Act, Families First Act, or the 2021 COVID relief law to sue the violator in federal district court, no matter what other law says [S2] [S3].

Suspends pre-dispute arbitration agreements and class-action waivers for employment, consumer, antitrust, and civil rights disputes for the covered emergency period plus 180 days, and puts courts rather than arbitrators in charge of deciding whether the suspension applies [S3].

The employment-dispute definition covers workers whether they are classified as employees or independent contractors, and preserves collective bargaining arbitration while barring it from waiving rights under constitutions or statutes [S3].
The bill preserves voluntary arbitration after a dispute arises, so it targets only clauses signed before a dispute exists [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Employers, consumer-facing companies, credit and investment providers, and the arbitration industry lose the enforceability of forced arbitration clauses during the emergency period, and anyone who violated the COVID relief laws faces individual lawsuits for the harm caused [S2] [S3].
analysis.who_pays_short: Employers, consumer-facing firms, and the arbitration industry

drawbacks.text: The new cause of action is written broadly — against 'any person' who violates or fails to comply with 'a requirement' of three large, detailed relief laws — which could produce a wave of litigation over technical compliance issues and add load to federal courts [S3].

The arbitration suspension applies retroactively to disputes that arose after the emergency began, so contracts signed before the bill would be affected, and companies would face uncertainty over which existing agreements remain enforceable [S3].

A good-faith objection from the employer and business side is that arbitration can be faster and cheaper than court for resolving individual disputes, and that suspending it even temporarily shifts costs onto employers and, potentially, consumers through higher prices [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core trade-off is real: reopening courtroom access and class actions for workers and consumers during the pandemic costs companies predictability and could crowd courts. But the relief laws the bill would enforce had already created obligations without a clear private right to enforce them, and the arbitration suspension is temporary rather than permanent, which limits the disruption companies would face.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Judiciary Committee and then to its Constitution subcommittee, and nothing further ever happened before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Janice Schakowsky introduced the bill in the House on January 28, 2021, with 13 Democratic cosponsors, and it was referred to the House Committee on the Judiciary [S1] [S4] [S5].

On March 22, 2021, it was referred to the Subcommittee on the Constitution, Civil Rights, and Civil Liberties, where it remained; no hearing, markup, committee vote, or floor action is recorded in its action history [S5].
No Republican cosponsors appear on the bill's cosponsor list; all 13 cosponsors are Democrats [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers and consumer-facing companies that rely on pre-dispute arbitration clauses keep their ability to channel disputes into individual arbitration, and anyone exposed to potential suits under the COVID relief laws faces no new private cause of action. Workers and consumers gained nothing from the bill's death.

for.name: Rep. Janice Schakowsky
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to create a COVID relief law cause of action and suspend pre-dispute arbitration

against.name: House Judiciary Committee
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to a hearing, markup, or vote; it sat referred after March 22, 2021 until the Congress ended

against.name: Subcommittee on the Constitution, Civil Rights, and Civil Liberties
against.what_they_did: Held the bill at subcommittee referral with no recorded action

sides.party_line_note: The bill's sponsor and all 13 cosponsors were House Democrats, and no Republican cosponsors appear in the record [S4].

industries.industry: Employers that use pre-dispute arbitration agreements
industries.note: The bill would make mandatory arbitration clauses and class-action waivers unenforceable for employment disputes during the covered emergency period, giving workers court access and collective action. The industry's interest in keeping forced arbitration runs against workers' courtroom rights.

industries.industry: Consumer-facing businesses, credit and investment providers
industries.note: Consumer and antitrust disputes could no longer be forced into individual arbitration during the emergency period, and violations of COVID relief laws would expose companies to private lawsuits for consumer harm.

Employment, consumer, antitrust, and civil rights cases would flow to courts instead of paid arbitrators for the duration of the emergency period plus 180 days, shrinking the caseload the industry handles.
